subject: Follow-up: Reliability SLO comparison & next tests
messages:

Subject: Follow-up: Reliability SLO comparison & next tests

Hi Tom / Samantha,

Thanks again for the call earlier — great context on Acme's production constraints. Per our discussion, I wanted to summarize the high-level differences we discussed between Redwood and the major hyperscalers when it comes to reliability & SLOs, and propose concrete next tests so we can validate at your scale.

Quick recap (high level):
- Uptime: Redwood offers SLA-backed uptime for Dedicated customers and regional failover for Hosted customers; typical targets we operate against are 99.95% (hosted) and 99.99% (dedicated SLA) with automated cross-region fallback.
- Rate limits / throttling: Redwood supports per-API-key and per-route rate limits with graceful queuing and backpressure instead of hard 429s in many configurations. Hyperscalers often use strict 429-based throttling at the infra layer for managed endpoints unless you provision dedicated capacity.
- Error budgets & observability: We provide token-level latency/cost breakdowns and per-route error budget dashboards so you can see degradation before it hits your SLA.
- Failover behavior: For our hosted flow we can configure automated fallback to a compatible model variant in a different region; Dedicated customers can set multi-region pools for active-passive failover.

Proposed next tests (to compare apples->apples):
1) Sustained throughput run: 500 req/s sustained for 1 hour to validate latency 95/99th distributions and tail behavior.
2) Rate-limit boundary: Gradually increase to breach quota to observe 429 behavior vs queued requests and our retry guidance.
3) Failover test: Simulate region outage and validate service continuity to a secondary region (observe cold-start behavior and cache warmup).
4) Error-budget burn: Introduce elevated error rates (50% errors on a subset) for a short window to observe circuit-breaker behavior and routing fallback.

Attachments I've included: redwood-slo-matrix.pdf (SLO comparison table), api-compare.csv (endpoint behaviors), and a draft mutual action plan (acme-mutual-action-plan.xlsx).

Next steps: can you confirm the following so we can schedule the POC?
- Preferred window for the sustained throughput / failover tests (dates/times in your timezone)
- A test API key or staging traffic target we can point the tests at (we can also run from our staging environment if you prefer)
- Which of these tests you want us to run vs you running from your perf team (we're happy to co-run)

I CC'd Ben to map the test details to our runbook and Aditya for any pricing/credit questions.

Thanks,

Marissa

Hi Marissa,

Thanks for the clear recap — helpful. A few clarifying items from our side before we lock dates:

- Throughput: 500 req/s looks right for an initial test, but can Redwood sustain 1k req/s in a burst test? We want to understand sustained vs burst behavior.
- Failover: when you do cross-region fallback, do you preserve in-flight requests / KV cache for chat-like workloads or do we expect a cold-start hit?
- Rate limits: our current architecture retries on 429s with exponential backoff; we'd prefer behavior that relies less on retries if possible (we've seen cascading failures on other providers). How does Redwood surface queued requests vs hard 429s in practice?

If you can answer those and propose a couple windows next week we can get our infra team (Samantha and two from SRE) on the calendar.

Tom

Hi Tom / Samantha — Ben here (engineering lead on customers/benchmarking). Quick answers and a proposed execution plan below.

Burst vs sustained:
- We can run a sustained 500 req/s for 1 hour and a separate burst test at 1k req/s for 5-10 minutes. For Hosted customers, sustained high throughput is a function of available capacity and routing policy — for Dedicated we guarantee throughput per the reserved pool.

Failover and KV cache behavior:
- Cross-region fallback does not preserve in-memory KV caches (there will be a cold-warm window). In practice we mitigate this with prefix caching and progressive warmup: the first 30-60s after failover shows higher latencies while cache populates. We'll measure the tail latencies during that window. Dedicated multi-region configs can be set up with warmed standby nodes to reduce the cold-start effect — we can include that in a Dedicated eval if you want.

Rate limits and queuing:
- Our standard hosted behavior is configurable: we offer soft-queueing where requests are buffered and served (up to a configurable buffer) with backpressure headers; once the buffer is exhausted requests receive 429. We also expose per-key and per-route headers so you can instrument retries correctly. For critical flows we recommend Dedicated capacity or a reserved burst policy to avoid relying on client-side retries.

Error budget / circuit breakers:
- We surface error-budget burn on the Console and can trigger automated routing changes (e.g., shift to a lower-cost model variant or alternate region) when thresholds are met. We'll run an error-injection experiment and show the console timeline during the test.

Proposed test plan & schedule:
- Wed 2026-03-25 10:00-12:00 PT: Sustained 500 req/s + 1k burst (5m)
- Thu 2026-03-26 02:00-03:00 PT: Failover test (we'll coordinate a controlled region failover)
- Thu 2026-03-26 03:00-04:00 PT: Error-budget injection (short window)

What we need from Acme:
- A staging endpoint or a flag to point test traffic at (API key or DNS CNAME)
- Preferred contact for SRE coordination (I see Samantha listed)
- Confirmation if you want us to run from Redwood-managed test agents or if you'll run from your infra (we can do both)

I've attached the SLO comparison matrix and the mutual action plan; runbook and test scripts are at https://docs.redwood.ai/slo-runbook. We'll also snapshot detailed latency histograms and request traces so you can compare to your hyperscaler runs.

Aditya — hop in on pricing/credits; we've budgeted a small pilot credit for this POC but want to confirm margins.

Thanks,

Ben
